court: The lord's manorial court (court baron), including Tooting and Wantage in the Bec rolls.
judges: The suitors, tenants who owe suit of court, give judgment according to Maitland's Introduction; the entries name no judge.
begins: A private plaint: a tenant sues another, for example for crop damage by animals or a 16d debt, and produces supporting witnesses (suit); the defendant is under pledges.
proof: A defendant denying the whole claim goes to his law with oath-helpers. The Tooting entry gives five compurgators (sixth hand); numbers in the other cases are not stated. These entries use no jury.

sources.title: Maitland, Select Pleas in Manorial and Other Seignorial Courts, vol. 1, Introduction (about pp. xi-xli) and Bec rolls 1246-1248 (Tooting, Wantage)
Pollock & Maitland, History of English Law, 2nd ed., vol. 2, pp. 212-214

note: data/procedures/SOURCES.md: rolls of 1246-1248 and a general 13th-century custom; use c. 1300 is an inference. The entries name no presiding officer; Maitland argues the steward toured with the rolls, but the suitors judged. Appeal/removal is not stated; no removal occurs in these entries. The Introduction (about p. xvii) says only that a writ of right had to begin in the lord's court. P&M describes royal debt practice c. 1300: without a sealed document a defendant could wage law; its disputed royal oath-helper counts are not applied here. Printed page numbers are approximate in the extracted scans.
